newsitem.title: UK: 2,000-year-old rat bones confuse N Zealand history.
newsitem.headline: 2,000-year-old rat bones confuse N Zealand history.

text.p: Rats started settling in New Zealand -- and munching their way through its unique wildlife -- more than 1,000 years before the first recorded human immigrants, scientists reported on Wednesday.
They said their findings meant that either humans started visiting earlier than believed or the rats got there some other way.
Richard Holdaway of Palaecol Research in Christchurch, New Zealand analysed rat bones found on both of New Zealand's islands using radiocarbon dating.
"The results show that 15 Pacific rat dates are significantly older than the generally accepted date for permanent human settlement," he wrote in a letter to the science journal Nature.

Rats had been widely believed to have arrived with the first human settlers of New Zealand about 850 years ago. They, and the other predators that arrived with people, are blamed for driving animals and birds like the moa into extinction, and putting kiwis and the parrot-like kakapos on the endangered list.
New Zealand's fauna evolved without mammal predators, and it once abounded with large, tasty, flightless birds.
But Holdaway said the 2,000-year-old rat bones probably meant people visited the islands earlier than thought.

"The rat is unlikely to have arrived without human assistance, on, for example, natural rafts. It is more likely that rats were introduced by transient human visitors, who either left immediately or quickly died out," he wrote.
